Infinitude of Primes. There is no largest prime number. The sequence of primes continues forever. Euclid proved this around 300 BCE using a proof by contradiction, establishing one of the earliest and most elegant results in number theory. Euclid's proof assumes a finite list of all primes, multiplies them together, adds one, and shows the result cannot be divisible by any prime on the list, proving either a new prime exists or demonstrating a gap in the list. For any prime p, another prime exists that is larger. The theorem has inspired multiple independent proofs over centuries, including arguments by Fermat, Euler, and modern variants using the divergence of the harmonic series over primes. The distribution of primes becomes sparser as numbers grow larger, yet their infinite supply guarantees they never cease. This foundational result anchors higher number theory and explains why prime-finding remains computationally relevant even for astronomically large numbers. The theorem connects to the Prime Number Theorem, which describes the asymptotic density of primes and refines how rarely they appear as numbers grow. It underpins the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, which depends on the existence and uniqueness of primes. The Riemann Hypothesis makes a deep conjecture about the distribution of infinitely many primes, refining what we know about their spacing. The Twin Prime Conjecture asks whether infinitely many pairs of primes exist, probing a special subset of this infinite supply.
